title: Fix the Beads false-staleness bug that killed the fleet w25 supervisor
what_this_does: Beads keeps issues in two places: a SQLite database and the issues.jsonl text file that git syncs. A safety gate refuses to run when it thinks the two disagree, but it judges by file timestamps, so the daemon's own rewrites constantly trip it on healthy repos — that false alarm killed the w25 supervisor. This plan makes the gate compare actual content instead of clocks, routes every writer of the file through one publisher that records a content hash before and after each atomic replace, adds the matching record step after every import, and stops the daemon's once-per-second rewrite loop. Then it rebuilds bd, installs it, and proves the fix live on the fleet repo.
why_bother: The false alarm has already cost a full supervisor run (w25 spent days in manual fallback) and it can kill any future orchestrator run on any repo with a beads daemon. True divergence detection is kept: only bytes written by someone else can trip the gate.

flow.label: Build the publisher package
flow.detail: internal/jsonlpub: freshness check, serialized publish, import record; failpoint tests for every crash state.

flow.label: Route all readers and writers
flow.detail: Six file writers and every import path go through the one package; the daemon loop's missing cleanup lands here.

flow.label: Prove it end to end
flow.detail: Scripted scratch-repo test on the new binary: loop dead, same-bytes rewrite fresh, real divergence still refused.

flow.label: Deploy
flow.detail: Stop the 7 bd daemons with bd's own stop command, install the new binary by rename, verify live on fleet; daemons relaunch on demand.

flow.label: Decide
flow.detail: Approve or send back through the page rail.

approving.plain: The staleness check will compare what the file actually contains against what the database recorded, so touching or rewriting the file with identical content can never again trigger the out-of-sync failure.
approving.detail: CheckStaleness and hasJSONLChanged both delegate to jsonlpub.ContentState: file sha256 vs the committed hash (jsonl_content_hash) and a new pending hash (jsonl_pending_hash). Verified live: fleet's stored hash d1df2880… already equals the file's sha256 exactly where the old mtime check false-fired.

approving.plain: Every program that writes or imports the issues file will go through one shared code path that keeps the file and its record consistent at every instant, even across crashes.
approving.detail: Publish: lock → divergence guard → dirty-first snapshot → temp write → pending hash → guard re-check → rename → promote → conditional dirty clear. RecordImport is the import-side twin committing the hash of the bytes actually parsed. Six writers routed (daemon export/flush/sync, autoflush, bd sync, bd export default path, RPC canonical path); custom-path exports stay plain.

approving.plain: The daemon bug that rewrote the file once per second forever gets the one missing cleanup call, so the race window stops recurring.
approving.detail: The pre-import flush at cmd/bd/daemon_sync.go:569-583 finally clears the dirty rows it exports (marked_at-conditional, so a mutation made mid-export is never silently lost), plus a divergence branch so a pulled file imports instead of starving.

approving.plain: The new bd binary replaces the installed one and the running daemons are stopped with bd's own command; they restart themselves on demand, as agreed at lock-in.
approving.detail: Backup kept at ~/.local/bin/bd.cd33f0f3.bak; install by rename (immune to text-file-busy); live probes on fleet: touch + info exits 0, daemon quiet over 60 s, true divergence still refused. Rollback is seconds: stop daemons, rename the backup over.

approving.plain: Four Codex review rounds shaped this plan; the final round's ten fixes are applied but had no further review round, which is disclosed as a risk with the test suite as backstop.
approving.detail: Trajectory of accepted findings: 11 → 11 → 12 → 10 across rounds, moving from design gaps to implementation precision. The Phase 1 failpoint tests exercise every final-round mechanism (guard re-check, starvation branch, lock-held sampler, cancellation) before any caller migrates.

rejected.idea: Upgrade to upstream Beads v1.x (Dolt), which deleted this whole design
rejected.why: It is one architecture away, not three versions: 109 local fork commits, the wt-merge JSONL lanes, and the orchestrator's bd integration all assume the current design. Recorded as a separate future work item candidate; you chose to fix the local fork now.

rejected.idea: Bake BD_ALLOW_STALE / no-daemon armor into supervise-launch.sh
rejected.why: That treats the alarm, not the lie. With staleness meaning real content divergence, the emergency overrides used during w25 become unnecessary.

rejected.idea: Persistent crash-evidence files to close the last theoretical gap
rejected.why: The gap needs a mid-crash publish followed by a byte-exact manual restore before any locked operation — two rarities in sequence, self-correcting at the next publish or import. Standing state costs more than the transient; documented as a revisit-if-observed risk.

risks.risk: The final review round's ten fixes went into v5 without another Codex pass (the 4-round ceiling).
risks.response: Every one of those mechanisms is covered by the Phase 1 protocol tests that must pass before any caller migrates; a test-revealed design flaw comes back as a defect, not a workaround.

risks.risk: Every freshness check now hashes the file (mtime shortcut removed).
risks.response: The codebase already accepted this cost for auto-import (bd-v0y: 10-50 ms worst case); fleet's 811 KB file hashes in under a millisecond.

risks.risk: The conditional dirty-clear depends on the SQLite driver round-tripping timestamps exactly.
risks.response: A dedicated Phase 1 test proves insert → snapshot → conditional delete on the real driver before anything relies on it.

risks.risk: A publisher wedged inside the lock could briefly block readers that saw a mismatch.
risks.response: Lock hold is milliseconds; acquisition is context-aware so RPC deadlines interrupt it; the steady-state fresh path never locks.
